questions.stem: Which term describes an investment company that is organized under a trust indenture, does not have a board of directors, and issues only redeemable securities representing an undivided interest in a unit of specified securities?
questions.explanation: The Investment Company Act of 1940 §4 defines a UIT as an investment company organized under a trust indenture, lacking a board of directors, and issuing only redeemable securities representing an undivided interest in a unit of specified securities. A management company (open- or closed-end) does have a board.

questions.stem: Which term describes a management company that is offering for sale, or has outstanding, any redeemable security of which it is the issuer?
questions.explanation: Under §5 of the Investment Company Act of 1940, an open-end company is defined as a management company that offers or has outstanding a redeemable security. Closed-end companies issue non-redeemable shares that trade in the secondary market.

questions.stem: A program that provides for flow-through tax consequences regardless of the legal entity used — for example an oil and gas, real estate, or agricultural limited partnership — is best described as a:
questions.explanation: FINRA Rule 2310 defines a direct participation program as one providing flow-through tax consequences, including oil and gas, real estate, and agricultural programs. REITs are expressly excluded from the DPP definition.

questions.stem: Which term identifies a municipal security issued by an issuer that, but for the application of Section 2(b) of the Investment Company Act of 1940, would constitute an investment company?
questions.explanation: MSRB Rule D-12 defines a "Municipal Fund Security" exactly in those terms. 529 plans, LGIPs, and ABLE programs are the classic examples. GO and revenue bonds are conventional debt obligations, not investment-company-like products.

questions.stem: The reduced sales charge available on a mutual fund purchase when the dollar amount invested reaches a specified level is known as a:
questions.explanation: A breakpoint is the dollar level at which the sales charge on investment company shares is reduced. A letter of intent is a written commitment to reach a breakpoint, and ROA aggregates prior holdings; both are mechanisms to qualify for breakpoints, but the discount level itself is the breakpoint.

questions.stem: Which term describes an option contract under which the holder has the right to purchase the number of units of the underlying security covered by the contract?
questions.explanation: FINRA Rule 2360 defines a "call" as an option contract under which the holder has the right to purchase the underlying. A put gives the right to sell. Warrants and rights are issuer-issued equity instruments, not standardized listed options.

questions.stem: A management company that has at least 75% of its assets in cash, government securities, securities of other investment companies, and other securities limited (per issuer) to not more than 5% of total assets and 10% of the issuer's voting securities is classified as a:
questions.explanation: §5(b)(1) of the Investment Company Act sets out the 75-5-10 test that defines a diversified management company. A non-diversified company is any management company that does not meet those thresholds.

questions.stem: Which term refers to the asset-based annual fee charged by an open-end fund to cover distribution and shareholder servicing expenses, paid out of fund assets pursuant to a written plan?
questions.explanation: SEC Rule 12b-1 under the Investment Company Act authorizes an open-end fund to use fund assets to pay distribution expenses pursuant to a written plan; the resulting charge is the "12b-1 fee." Front-end loads and CDSCs are sales charges paid by the investor at purchase/redemption, not asset-based distribution fees.

questions.stem: An issuer that is engaged primarily in the business of investing, reinvesting, or trading in securities — or that owns investment securities exceeding 40% of total assets (exclusive of government securities and cash items) — meets the statutory definition of a(n):
questions.explanation: Section 3(a) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 defines an "investment company" using these primary-engagement and 40% investment-securities tests. The other choices are unrelated regulated entities.

questions.stem: Which term describes a hedge-fund-type pooled vehicle that is typically organized as a limited partnership, requires a high minimum investment, and is generally illiquid?
questions.explanation: Per the SIE outline, hedge funds are characterized by a high minimum investment, partnership structure, and general illiquidity. Mutual funds and ETFs are registered, liquid pooled vehicles, and a UIT issues redeemable units of a fixed portfolio.

questions.stem: Which term identifies an exchange-traded product that is an unsecured debt obligation of an issuer whose return is linked to the performance of a specified index or benchmark?
questions.explanation: An ETN is an unsecured debt instrument whose return tracks a referenced index; an ETF is a pooled investment that holds a portfolio of securities. Closed-end funds and REITs are equity-based investment vehicles.

questions.stem: Which term describes a real estate investment vehicle that distributes the bulk of its taxable income to shareholders and thereby avoids taxation at the entity level, providing tax-advantaged income without double taxation?
questions.explanation: The SIE outline identifies REITs as vehicles that pass income to shareholders and avoid double taxation when distribution requirements are met. C-corporations are taxed at both the entity and shareholder level; ETNs are debt instruments; face-amount certificate companies are a separate class of investment company.
